column2: Then the mighty Skanda shone as general, lord and protector of the gods, doing what was dear to Shankara.
This blessed son of Pavaka, golden in form, ever the boy, attained the generalship of the gods.
Therefore gold is auspicious, the best and imperishable jewel, the innate splendour of Kartikeya and the highest splendour of fire.
Thus, Kauravya, Vasishtha told Rama long ago; therefore strive to give gold, lord of men.
Rama, having given gold, was freed from all sin and gained a great place in the third heaven, not easy for men.
[Vaishampayana said:] Thus addressed by Yudhishthira, Bhishma, Shantanu's son, began to tell this entire rule of the funeral rite.
[Bhishma said:] Hear attentively, king, this auspicious rule of the funeral rite, bringing wealth, fame and sons, the sacrifice to the ancestors, scorcher of foes.
Ancestors are always to be honoured by gods, asuras and men, gandharvas, serpents and rakshasas, pishachas and kinnaras.
They honour the ancestors first and afterward satisfy the gods; therefore a man should always honour them with all effort.
The Anvaharya rite for ancestors, great king, is said to be that done with meat by rule; this rule was first ordained.
On all days the grandfathers are pleased by funeral rites done; I shall tell you the qualities and faults of each lunar day.
The fruit gained by funeral rites done on those days, sinless one: all that I shall tell, as it is; hear it from me.
Honouring the ancestors on the first day, one would gain in his house women, handsome, bearing children, to be admired, with many offspring.
Those who do it on the fifth day, king, have many sons born; those who do it on the sixth become sharers in splendour.
One doing the rite on the seventh, king, becomes a sharer in farming; one doing it on the eighth gains profit in trade.
One who does the rite on the ninth has many single-hoofed animals; for those who perform funeral rites on the tenth, cows increase.
A mortal doing it on the eleventh, king, becomes a sharer in vessels and metals, and sons of Brahmic splendour are born in his house.
For one who strives on the twelfth, much silver and lovely gold are constantly seen.
One doing the rite on the thirteenth becomes best among his kinsmen, but young men in his house surely die.
A mortal doing the rite on the fourteenth becomes a sharer in battle; offering on the new moon, he would gain all desires.
In the dark fortnight, from the tenth onward, except the fourteenth, the lunar days are praised for funeral rites, not the others.
As the latter fortnight is distinguished above the former, so afternoon is distinguished above forenoon for the funeral rite.
[Bhishma said:] The offerings in the rule of the funeral rite that knowers of the rite know: hear from me those, Yudhishthira, the desired ones, and their fruit.
With sesame, rice, barley, beans, water, roots and fruits given for a month, the ancestors are pleased by the funeral rite, king.
Manu said that a funeral rite with growing sesame is imperishable; and in all foods sesame is remembered as chief.
Satisfaction of the host of ancestors is two months with fish, they say three months with mutton, four months with hare.
With goat's meat the ancestors are pleased five months, king; with boar's six months, and with birds' seven.
Eight months with Parshata, nine with Raurava, and a satisfaction of ten months with the meat of the gavaya.
Eleven months is the ancestors' pleasure with buffalo; with the cow's, a year is said here for the offering given.
As cow's, so is payasa with ghee; with the meat of the vadhrinasa the satisfaction is twelve years.
May he be born in our family who gives on the thirteenth, under the Maghas in the southern course, payasa joined with ghee.
Or with goat's meat or iron-vessel offering under the Maghas, of controlled vow, duly in the elephant's shadow, fanned with the ear's fan.
Many sons are to be desired, so that even one may go to Gaya, where the banyan, the maker of imperishability, is famed in the worlds.
Water, roots, fruit, meat or food at the ancestors' rite, whatever mixed with honey, makes for endlessness.
The man who always does the funeral rite under the conjunction of Krittika, having kindled the fires, would sacrifice with offspring, free of fever.
Wishing offspring, under Rohini; wishing vigour, under Mrigashiras; one who gives a funeral rite under Ardra becomes a doer of cruel deeds.
A mortal doing the rite under Punarvasu becomes a sharer in farming; wishing nourishment, a man should seek the funeral rite under Pushya.
Giving the rite under Ashlesha, he begets hero sons; offering the rite under the Maghas he becomes the best among his kinsmen.
Giving the funeral rite under the Phalgunis, the giver becomes fortunate; under Uttara a sharer in offspring; under Hasta a sharer in fruit.
Giving the rite under Chitra he would gain handsome sons; honouring ancestors at the conjunction of Svati, he lives by trade.
A man striving for the ancestors' rite under Vishakha has many sons; doing it under Anuradha he would set a wheel of kingship going.
A man going to overlordship, renouncing under Jyeshtha, best of the Kurus, funeral rites precede at Yama's city.
Doing the funeral rite under Abhijit he would gain the best learning; giving it under Shravana he would go after death to the highest goal.
A man gains a share in kingship under Dhanishtha and does not meet calamity; doing it under the Varuna star, a physician would gain success.
Doing it under Purva Proshthapada he would gain many goats and sheep; doing it under Uttara he gains cows by the thousand.
He gains wealth made of many silvers under Revati; he gains horses under Ashvayuj; and under the Bharanis the best life.
Hearing this rule of the funeral rite, Shashabindu did so, and without trouble conquered and ruled the earth.
[Bhishma said:] A kshatriya who knows the dharma of giving should not examine brahmanas; but in the rite for the gods and ancestors examination is called just.
People worship the gods here by divine splendour alone; therefore a man should have it given to all gods.
But at a funeral rite, great king, the wise should examine brahmanas by family, conduct, age, form, learning and lineage.
Of these, some defile the row and others purify the row; hear, king, I shall tell of those who are not fit for the row.
A gambler, a killer of an embryo, a consumptive, a herdsman, one outside the form, a servant of others, a usurer, a singer, a seller of everything,
an arsonist, a poisoner, one who eats at the kunda, a seller of Soma, a sea-voyager, a king's servant, an oil-presser, a forger,
one who quarrels with his father, he in whose house is an adulterer, one accused, a thief, and one who lives by craft,
a festival-maker, a needle-worker, a betrayer of friends, an adulterer, a teacher of those without vows, and one with arrow-back.
Know these here as unfit for the row, the lowest of the twice-born, and those of little mind who give instruction to shudras.
A one-eyed man defiles sixty, a eunuch a hundred, and a leper as far as he sees, king, when seated in a row.
Know all to be demonic that is eaten with the head wrapped, eaten facing south, or eaten wearing sandals.
What is given with envy and what is devoid of faith, Brahma ordained all that as a share for the lord of asuras.
Dogs and row-defilers should not look on in any way; therefore one should give in a screened place and scatter sesame.
At the scattering of sesame, flesh-eaters and the hosts of Krodhavasha, yatudhanas and pishachas plunder that offering.
As far as an unfit man sees those eating in a row, so far he causes the giver of that to fall from the fruit, the fool.
But these, best of the Bharatas, are to be known as row-purifiers; whom I shall now tell, examine those twice-born here.
All brahmanas who are bathed in Vedic learning and vows are fit for the row; but those I shall tell are to be known as row-purifiers.
A Trinachiketa, a Panchagni, a Trisuparna, a knower of the six limbs, one whose line is a giver of Brahman, a Chhandogya, a singer of the Jyeshtha Sama,
one who is obedient to mother and father, a Shrotriya of ten generations, one who approaches his lawful wives in season: a brahmana bathed in Vedic learning and vow purifies the row.
A student of the Atharvashiras, a celibate of controlled vow, truthful, dharmic in character and devoted to his own work,
and those who have toiled at ablutions in holy sacred fords and at sacrifices with mantras and have been bathed in the concluding bath.

The angerless, the steady, the patient, the self-controlled, masters of senses, and those who are good to all beings: one should invite these to funeral rites. A gift to them is imperishable; they are row-purifiers.
These others also, great king, are to be known as row-purifiers: ascetics who know the dharma of liberation, yogis of well-practised vows,
those who, restrained, make the best of the twice-born hear the Itihasa, and those who know commentaries and those devoted to grammar,
those who study the Purana and the law books and, having studied rightly, act by rule,
one who has lived in his teacher's house, truthful, giver of thousands, chief in all Vedas and all recitations.
As far as these see in a row, so far they purify; therefore from that purifying of the row he is called a row-purifier.
One alone may purify for two and a half krosha: so the knowers of Brahman know, "one whose line is a giver of Brahman".
One who is no officiant and no teacher, if he goes to the first seat, not permitted by officiants, takes the row's misdeed.
But if a knower of the Veda, free of all row-faults, is not fallen, king, he is a row-purifier indeed.
Therefore with all effort one should examine and invite the twice-born devoted to their own work, self-controlled, of good family and of much learning.
He for whom funeral rites and offerings are chiefly for friends does not please ancestors and gods and does not go to heaven.
One who makes friendships at funeral rites does not go by the path of the gods; freed from bondage like a fig fruit, the friend of funeral rites falls from the world of heaven.

Therefore one doing a funeral rite should not favour a friend; he should give wealth to friends for gathering; one who is thought neither enemy nor friend, that neutral one should be fed at rites for gods and ancestors.
As seed sown in barren soil does not sprout and the sower does not get a share of seed, so a funeral rite eaten by the unworthy gives fruit neither here nor hereafter.
A brahmana who does not study dies out like a straw fire; the funeral rite should not be given to him, for it is not poured in ash.
The fee called "sambhojani" is a fee for pishachas; it goes neither to gods nor to ancestors; it wanders here with merit exhausted, like a cow that has lost her calf between houses.
As ghee is offered in extinguished fire, it goes neither to gods nor ancestors; so what is given to a dancer or singer, and the fee that is taken by one without the Rik.
It hurts both and does not feed; the fee given to one without the Rik is a slaying, a blamed thing that falls; it would make the dead fall from the path of the gods.
Those who constantly follow the agreement of the sages, resolved, knowing all dharma: the gods know them as brahmanas.
Sages devoted to study, devoted to knowledge, devoted to austerity and devoted to action are to be known, Bharata.
Offerings for ancestors are to be established with those devoted to knowledge, Bharata; there brahmanas who do not blame are the best.
But those who blame in conversations should not be fed at funeral rites; blamed brahmanas, king, would destroy a family of three generations.
The word of the Vaikhanasa sages is heard, king: one should examine from afar brahmanas who have crossed the Veda, whether dear or hated; to them one should offer that funeral rite.
One man who would feed a thousand thousand without the Rik: one who knows mantra, pleased, deserves all of them, Bharata.
[Yudhishthira said:] What is to be avoided at funeral rites, and roots and fruits, and what kind of grain is to be avoided? Tell me, grandfather.
[Bhishma said:] Hear from me, lord of men, how the funeral rite arose, in what time, of what nature, and who resolved it.
Svayambhuva Atri, Kauravya, the supreme sage of great power; in his line, great king, was Dattatreya.
Dattatreya's son was the ascetic Nimi, and Nimi had a son, glorious, named Shrimat, enveloped in prosperity.
At the end of a thousand years, having done hard austerity, he met his end, his mind seized by the law of time.
Nimi, having done the purifications by the rule seen, was filled with fierce torment, devoted to grief for his son.
Then the very wise one, having made offerings on the fourteenth, counting that grief, awoke in the night.
As he woke, his self covered by grief, his mind withdrew from the object and his understanding spread wide.
On the new moon, greatly wise one, having brought honoured brahmanas, he himself made all the seats right-turning.
Then he brought seven brahmanas together for the meal; the lord gave them food without salt, shyamaka grain.
Then kusha grass with tips to the south was placed on the seats and at the feet of the brahmanas who ate the food.
Having made the kusha grass with tips to the south, very restrained and pure, he gave the rice-ball to the glorious one, uttering name and gotra.
Having done that, that best of sages, afterward tormented by great remorse over the mixture of dharma by himself, reflected:
What was done by me that was not done by sages before? How would brahmanas not burn me by a curse?
Then he thought of the founder of his line; and Atri, the ascetic, came at his mere thought.
Seeing him so, wasted by grief for his son, the imperishable Atri greatly comforted him with welcome words:

This sacrifice for the ancestors, Nimi, was resolved by you, ascetic; do not be afraid; this dharma was seen before and ordained by Brahma himself.

mahabharata:13:91.28	Honoured by the funeral rite, they are freed from stain; the seven-fold line of the ancestors was seen before by the Self-born.

mahabharata:13:91.38	Grains unfit for funeral rites are kodrava and pulaka; among goods asafoetida, among vegetables onion and garlic,

Having so spoken to the sage of his line, the blessed ascetic Atri went to the divine assembly of the grandfather.
The sages, constant in dharma, having performed offerings, also made water-offerings, of controlled vow, with water from sacred fords.
Satisfied by offerings given by the four classes, Bharata, the ancestors and gods could not digest the food.
Oppressed by indigestion, those gods with the ancestors went to Soma, tormented by the offerings.
The ancestors, oppressed by indigestion, said to Soma: "We are tormented by the offering food; let something good be ordained here."
Then Soma replied to them, "Gods, if you wish the good, go to the Self-born's abode; he will ordain the good."
At Soma's word the gods with the ancestors, Bharata, came to the grandfather seated on Meru's peak.
[The ancestors said:] "We are greatly oppressed by the offering food, blessed one; show favour to us, god; let our good be ordained."
Hearing their words, the Self-born said: "Fire here at my side will ordain your good."
Hearing this, the ancestors became free of fever; for this reason, king, the first share is given to fire.
When the offering is made with Agni first, bull among men, brahma-rakshasas do not assail that offering, and rakshasas turn away when the god Vibhavasu stands there.
One should give the first rice-ball to the father, then to the grandfather and then to the great-grandfather; this is remembered as the rule of the funeral rite.
At the funeral rite one should say the Savitri, composed, with each rice-ball, and one should say "To Soma" and "To the one with ancestors".
A menstruating woman, one with deformed ears, should not attend the offering; those born of other lines are not to be accepted.
Crossing water, one should name the grandfathers; reaching a river, one should do the rice-ball and water-offering for ancestors.
First, having made the water-offering for those of one's own line, one should then give a water-offering to the group of friends and relatives.
For one crossing water in a yoke of dappled cows, ancestors wish; and for one climbing into a boat, water is given on the boat always, composed, by those who know.
In the second half of the dark fortnight one should make offerings; nourishment, long life, vigour and prosperity come to those who follow the ancestors.
The grandfather, Pulastya, Vasishtha, Pulaha, Angiras, Kratu and the great sage Kashyapa: these, best of the Kurus, are remembered as the great lords of yoga.
And these are the ancestors, king; this is the supreme rule of the funeral rite; the dead are freed from the bond of the rice-ball by that act.
Thus the origin of the funeral rite, according to tradition, best of men, has been told, as indicated before; now I shall tell of giving.
[Bhishma said:] Those who eat with vows not told in the Veda while doing their work, and those who eat with vows told in the Veda, have broken vows, Yudhishthira.
[Yudhishthira said:] What common people call austerity, fasting, is that austerity here, or what else would be austerity?
[Bhishma said:] One who does not fast two weeks or two months, whatever the people think austerity; one who harms himself by the rule of the self is neither an ascetic nor a knower of dharma.
And accomplishment in renunciation remains the highest austerity; one should be a constant faster and a celibate.
A brahmana should always be a sage and always worship the gods; a householder desiring dharma should always sleep, Bharata.
He should always eat nectar and always be pure; always speak of order and always be restrained.
He should always eat the remains and always love guests; he should always be a non-meat-eater and always pure.
[Yudhishthira said:] How can one be a constant faster and a celibate, king, how an eater of remains, and how fond of guests?
One who always eats after servants and guests have eaten eats only nectar: know this, Yudhishthira.
A man who does not eat when brahmanas have not eaten: by that not-eating his heaven is conquered.
One who eats what remains after gods, ancestors, servants and guests is called an eater of remains.
Their worlds are endless, remembered in Brahma's abode, attended by apsarases and gandharvas, lord of men.
They enjoy with gods and guests and with ancestors, and rejoice with sons and grandsons; their goal is unsurpassed.
[Bhishma said:] A twice-born who accepts from a good man and likewise from a bad man: with a gifted one there is little fault, but he sinks with a qualityless one.
On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of Vrishadarbhi and the seven sages, Bharata.
Kashyapa, Atri, Vasishtha, Bharadvaja, Gautama, Vishvamitra, Jamadagni and the virtuous Arundhati,
and their servant Ganda, and Pashusakha the shudra, her husband, were with them.
All of them, practising austerity, formerly roamed this earth, learning by concentration the eternal world of Brahma.
Then there was a great drought, descendant of the Kurus, when this world was hungry and its life hard.
In some sacrifice long ago, the sacrificed-for Shaibya's son Sibi's son was given as a fee to officiants, his own son.
At that time he, short-lived, met his fated end, and they, tormented by hunger, surrounded him.
As the king Shaibya Vrishadarbhi wandered, he saw them on the road cooking, wasted.
[Vrishadarbhi said:] "Receiving carries across, and nourishes those who receive. Hear, ascetics, what wealth I have.
A brahmana asking is dear to me; I would give you a thousand she-mules, each with bulls, all swift, white-haired, in breeding.
I give you families, hundreds of hundreds of oxen, fine yoke-bearers in every way, earth-carriers, stout, the best ploughers, cows of good vows.
Excellent villages, rice, barley, juices, jewels and other rare things: what shall I give? Do not make this feeling in me that I am to eat you; what shall I give you for your nourishment?"
[The sages said:] "King, a king's gift is like honey in taste but like poison; knowing that, why do you tempt us?
Kshatra is like a deity, relying on a brahmana; he is spotless, pleased with austerity, and pleases the gods.
Even in a day a brahmana's austerity is lost; a king's gift received burns it like a forest fire.
Welfare to you with your gift, king; let everything be given to those who ask." Having so said, they went away.
That meat of the wise ones remained uncooked; leaving it, they all went to the forest wishing food.
Then urged by the king, his ministers went to the forest, gathered udumbara fruits, and began to give them as a gift.
Servants brought other udumbara fruits with gold inside, and ran to make them accept.
Knowing them heavy, Atri said they were not to be accepted: "We are not fools of knowledge, nor dull-witted; we know these are gold; we are awake and aware.
What is taken here would have bitter results after death; this is not to be accepted by one wishing happiness here and hereafter."
[Vasishtha said:] "A nishka counted by a hundred, measured by a thousand; the more one accepts, the more one gains the sinful goal."
[Kashyapa said:] "Whatever rice, barley, gold, animals and women there are on earth, all of it is not enough for one man; therefore the learned should go to peace."
[Bharadvaja said:] "The horn of a ruru deer grows as it is born; so a man's longing grows; there is no measure to it."
[Gautama said:] "There is no wealth in the world that could fill the world; a man is like an ocean, never filled."
[Vishvamitra said:] "When the desire of one desiring desire is fulfilled, another desire, thirst, pierces him like an arrow."
[Jamadagni said:] "Restraint in accepting bears austerity firmly; a brahmana's austerity flows away if he is greedy."
[Arundhati said:] "The hoarding of goods for dharma, approved by the side, is austerity hoarding here, distinguished from hoarding goods."
[Ganda said:] "Fearing this fierce one, my lords here are afraid; I, like a weak one, fear more than they, hereafter."
[Pashusakha said:] "That for which there is nothing higher in dharma, brahmanas know as wealth; for the sake of discipline I would serve the very learned as they are."
[The sages said:] "Welfare with your gift to him whose subjects these are; you give us fruits joined with deceit."
[Bhishma said:] Having so said, those sages, firm in vows, leaving those gold-filled fruits, all went elsewhere.
If he should ask you by whom you were told of him, say 'By Narada', as if burning, scourge of foes.
Great sacrifices with ample fees, beautified with mountains of food, were performed; enjoyments were enjoyed, and sons were protected.
His eyes full of tears, broad-chested, mighty-armed Partha, more distressed than the distressed, took his feet, Bharata.
[Sauti said:] Thus addressed, the brahmana sage, permitted by the great soul Vyasa, began to tell the king.
